title: Allow customizing the configuration of the managed/embedded containerd instance
body:
### Description

When `dockerd` starts its own ("managed"/"embedded") containerd, there is no supported way to
customize that containerd's configuration. Everything is hardcoded in Go, and the generated config
file is overwritten on every daemon start.

**Current behavior**

`dockerd` builds the containerd config from a struct and serializes it to
`<exec-root>/containerd/containerd.toml` (i.e. `/var/run/docker/containerd/containerd.toml`),
truncating any existing file:

- `daemon/internal/libcontainerd/supervisor/remote_daemon.go`
  - `Start()` constructs `config.Config` with only `Version`, `Root`, `State`, `GRPC`, `Debug`.
  - `getContainerdConfig()` opens the file with `os.O_CREATE|os.O_TRUNC|os.O_WRONLY` and encodes the
    struct, so hand-edits are lost on the next `dockerd` restart (and on containerd restarts
    performed by the supervisor).
- `daemon/internal/libcontainerd/supervisor/remote_daemon_options.go`: the only knobs are
  `WithLogLevel`, `WithLogFormat`, `WithCRIDisabled`, `WithDetectLocalBinary`.
- `daemon/command/daemon.go` (`getContainerdDaemonOpts`): the only daemon.json field that influences
  this is `cri-containerd`.

Consequences:

1. **No drop-in support.** containerd's own default config sets
   `imports = [defaults.DefaultConfigIncludePattern]` (typically `/etc/containerd/conf.d/*.toml`),
   but the config generated by dockerd is built from an empty `Imports` field, so the drop-in
   directory is silently ignored for the managed instance.
2. **No per-plugin configuration.** There is no way to set anything under `[plugins.*]`, e.g.:
   - CRI runtime options such as `privileged_without_host_devices` /
     `privileged_without_host_devices_all_devices_allowed`
     (needed for VM/sandbox runtimes like Kata/gVisor, where bind-mounting all host devices into a
     "privileged" container is meaningless or unsafe; see also #39697 and
     `containerd/internal/cri/server/container_create.go`),
   - `proxy_plugins` (external snapshotters, see #47444),
   - registry/`config_path`, runtime `options`, `base_runtime_spec` (cf. #45819).
3. **Hardcoded values drift.** dockerd still disables CRI by the containerd v1 plugin URI
   (`io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri`), which no longer matches anything in containerd v2
   (`io.containerd.cri.v1.runtime` / `io.containerd.cri.v1.images`); this had to be patched
   separately in #53564 / #53585 — a symptom of the config being generated from hardcoded strings.

**Workarounds today (and why they are not enough)**

- Run a system containerd on `/run/containerd/containerd.sock`; dockerd detects it
  (`systemContainerdRunning`) and skips starting a managed one, so `/etc/containerd/config.toml`
  and `conf.d/*.toml` apply. This works, but it forces users to install and manage a second daemon
  (systemd unit, upgrades, rootless setups), and it is not viable for the static-binary/container
  images (e.g. `dind`) where the whole point of the managed instance is "just run dockerd".
- Hand-edit `/var/run/docker/containerd/containerd.toml`: lost on the next daemon start.

**Proposal (open to alternatives)**

Give users a supported way to inject configuration into the managed containerd, e.g. one of:

1. Write containerd's default `imports` (or a Docker-specific drop-in dir such as
   `/etc/docker/containerd.d/*.toml`) into the generated config, so users can ship drop-in files.
   Requires a documented precedence rule for fields dockerd must own (`root`, `state`, `grpc.address`).
2. Add an explicit daemon.json field, e.g. `"containerd-config": { ... }` (raw `plugins` map merged
   over the generated config), and/or `"containerd-config-file": "/etc/docker/containerd.toml"`
   used as a base config that dockerd merges its required values over.
3. At minimum, a `--containerd-config-path` flag so the generated file location (and thus a
   pre-seeded config) can be controlled.

Related: #43950 (use containerd's defaults), #45819 (base OCI spec override), #39697
(`privileged-without-host-devices`), #47444 (nix-snapshotter needs `proxy_plugins`),
#53564 / #53585 (CRI plugin URIs).

title: Health checks stop for good when a probe's exec finishes before cmdProbe.run reaches its first select
body:
### Description

On Docker 29.2.1, a container's health checks can stop permanently. No further check runs, and `State.Health` keeps its last result (`healthy`) indefinitely. Nothing is logged. Restarting dockerd (with live-restore) recovers; nothing else does.

We have seen it four times in 24 days on one host, on three different containers. Three of the four were the fastest checks: `redis-cli ping` every 10 s (twice), and `kill -0 $(cat /run/nginx.pid)` every 30 s. The fourth, a `wget` to a local HTTP endpoint every 30 s, is likely the same, but no dump was taken that time. The three caught with a dump each happened on a quiet host.

**Cause** (line numbers from `docker-v29.2.1`):

- [`health.go#L106`](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.2.1/daemon/health.go#L106) runs `ContainerExecStart` in a goroutine that sends its result to `execErr`, a channel with capacity 1.
- The first `select` ([L115–L124](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.2.1/daemon/health.go#L115-L124)) waits on the 30 s start timer, `execErr`, or `execConfig.Started`.
- `ContainerExecStart` closes `Started` ([`exec.go#L311`](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.2.1/daemon/exec.go#L311)) before it returns `nil` ([L341](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.2.1/daemon/exec.go#L341)).
- So if the exec has completed by the time `run` evaluates the first `select`, `Started` is closed and `execErr` holds `nil`. Both cases are ready, and Go picks one at random.
- When it picks `execErr`, `run` carries on as if the exec had only started. It resets the timer to the probe timeout and enters the second `select` ([L131](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.2.1/daemon/health.go#L131)), where `execErr` is now empty.
- The timeout fires, `cancelProbe()` runs, and `<-execErr` at [L137](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.2.1/daemon/health.go#L137) blocks forever, because the channel's only value was consumed by the first `select`.
- `monitor` waits on this probe's result ([L291](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.2.1/daemon/health.go#L291), [L308](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/docker-v29.2.1/daemon/health.go#L308)), so the container gets no further checks.

The goroutine dumps (excerpt under Additional Info) prove this path:

- `run` is at L137, which only the timeout branch of the second `select` reaches.
- No exec goroutine remains, so its result was sent, and something received it.
- That receive was the first `select`. An error there returns early, and a receive in the second `select` would have skipped L137.

The window needs the whole exec (start, run, exit) to finish before `run` evaluates its first `select`. That is why fast checks are the exposed ones. `cmdProbe.run` on `master` (checked 2026-10-09) has the same two `select`s; the only difference from 29.2.1 is a guard against an empty command.


### Reproduce

Not deterministic. What we run, and what we see:

1. A container with a fast health check, e.g. `redis:8.2.4-alpine` with `test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]`, `interval: 10s`, `timeout: 5s`, on a daemon with live-restore enabled.
2. Wait. Here it took between 15 hours and 8 days of daemon uptime.
3. `docker inspect <container> --format '{{range .State.Health.Log}}{{.End}} {{end}}'` stops advancing, while `.State.Health.Status` stays `healthy`.
4. `kill -USR1 $(pidof dockerd)` writes a goroutine dump in which:
   - the container's `monitor` goroutine waits at `health.go:308`, and its `cmdProbe.run` goroutine is in `chan receive` at `health.go:137`, both for as long as the checks have been stopped;
   - no goroutine created at `health.go:106` by that `run` goroutine exists.
5. `systemctl restart docker` brings the checks back.

A delay injected between `health.go` L106 and L115 should make it reproducible with any fast check; we have not tried it.


### Expected behavior

Health checks keep running every `interval`. When the first `select` in `cmdProbe.run` receives the exec's `nil` result, the check has already finished: its exit code should be recorded as the check's result, instead of the probe waiting on `execErr` a second time.

### docker version

```bash
 Git commit:        a5c7197
```


### Additional Info

**Goroutine dump** (2026-10-09, `SIGUSR1`, filtered to the goroutines that mention `health.go`, stuck container only):

```
goroutine 127 [select, 34 minutes]:
github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon.monitor(...)
        /root/build-deb/engine/daemon/health.go:308 +0x4f7
created by github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon.(*Daemon).updateHealthMonitor in goroutine 103
        /root/build-deb/engine/daemon/health.go:358 +0x10e
goroutine 253968 [chan receive, 34 minutes]:
github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon.(*cmdProbe).run(...)
        /root/build-deb/engine/daemon/health.go:137 +0x10d4
github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon.monitor.func2()
        /root/build-deb/engine/daemon/health.go:291 +0xde
created by github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon.monitor in goroutine 127
        /root/build-deb/engine/daemon/health.go:289 +0x488
```

The other containers' monitors sit idle at `health.go:280`, or have a check in flight (`health.go:131` plus a goroutine at `exec.go:318` created at `health.go:106`), as expected. Two earlier dumps show the same picture: 2026-10-06 (36 minutes) and 2026-10-08 (238 minutes).

**Suggested fix.** A `nil` from `execErr` in the first `select` means the exec has already exited, so skip the second `select` and read the exit code:

```go
	execDone := false
	select {
	case <-tm.C:
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("timed out starting health check for container %s", cntr.ID)
	case err := <-execErr:
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		// Started was closed as well: the exec has already exited, and its result
		// has just been consumed, so it must not be waited for again below.
		execDone = true
	case <-execConfig.Started:
		metrics.HealthCheckStartDuration.UpdateSince(startTime)
	}

	if !execDone {
		// existing timer reset and second select, unchanged
	}
```

#52450 (closed without merging) bounded the L137 wait with a 30 s timeout, for a different trigger (`ContainerExecStart` never returning). That bound would also turn this hang into one failed check, but the cause here is the consumed value.

**Environment.** `docker-ce` `5:29.2.1-1~ubuntu.24.04~noble`, `containerd.io` `2.2.1-1`, live-restore enabled, containerd snapshotter. Ubuntu 24.04 in an LXC container on Proxmox (kernel 6.17.4-2-pve), with 2 CPUs (`docker info`), so the Go runtime runs dockerd on two threads. The host was not CPU-throttled (cgroup `cpu.max` = `max`, `nr_throttled 0`) and lightly loaded at each freeze.

**Related:** #52330, #52450, #41871 (the same symptom, after a daemon restart), #37288 (the problem the two `select`s address).

title: custom selector like `--platform`
body:
### Description

one can build images using the platform parameter.
ex.: `build --platform=linux/amd64`  

these images can be bundled using manifests.
ex.: `manifest create [name, list, ...]`

at runtime the selector `platform` is read and according to the client machine the right image used to do action.
is there a possibility for a custom selector that can be supplied on the cli.

personally id prefer to use subject from the referral api. add a relationhship that can be addressed directly.
there is also the possibility to add annotations, which currently arent addressable but could be regarded as an alternative.

an exemplatory command would look like:
`run --platform=linux/amd64 --subject=test`

 if there is a feature like this. please let me know.

title: Container with volume type: image and subpath fails to start after dockerd restart
body:
### Description

Here is a simple docker compose with an image volume with a `subpath`. After a restart of dockerd (e.g. due to a system reboot) these containers fail to start. 

In the journal we see
`level=error msg="failed to start container" container=4a85b4a7dd1024f27ce2f6b1784fd0580d914ed6a9f09ae15032a21f8d5cacb8 error="cannot access path /var/lib/docker/overlay2/1c3e9bc58352ab72e892f188f5c7701e62093e2e8b67bd975cdcb6574d69d5b6/merged/usr: lstat /var/lib/docker/overlay2/1c3e9bc58352ab72e892f188f5c7701e62093e2e8b67bd975cdcb6574d69d5b6/merged/usr: no such file or directory"`

`docker compose up` fails with
```
Error response from daemon: cannot access path /var/lib/docker/overlay2/1c3e9bc58352ab72e892f188f5c7701e62093e2e8b67bd975cdcb6574d69d5b6/merged/usr: lstat /var/lib/docker/overlay2/1c3e9bc58352ab72e892f188f5c7701e62093e2e8b67bd975cdcb6574d69d5b6/merged/usr: no such file or directory
```
The issue can be resolved with a new container (`down` and `up`).

### Reproduce


- Unskip and run test:
https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/d7ffb12e5048ac19cd38330685f3d35ffbd9934f/integration/volume/mount_test.go#L426-L427

title: containerd changes endpoint walks unchanged lower trees without cancellation; high memory under concurrent requests
body:
# Upstream report: Docker containerd filesystem changes resource use

## Observed incident and source evidence

The reporter of [disk-space-saviour issue 22](https://github.com/link-foundation/disk-space-saviour/issues/22)
observed 22 concurrent changes requests against one Docker 29.6.1 container
using the containerd image store on an 11.7 GB Ubuntu 24.04 host. The kernel
reported dockerd anonymous RSS of 7,302,520 kB before killing it. Restarting
dockerd then terminated all task containers. The related
[profile](https://github.com/link-foundation/disk-space-saviour/issues/21)
records 2,022 seconds in 24 diffs of large image/build trees.

These are the original reporter's observations, not an OOM reproduced in this
checkout. This checkout's Docker daemon uses fuse-overlayfs, so it does not
reproduce the reported containerd backend. We intentionally did not run the
unbounded original reproduction on the shared host.

[ImageService.Changes](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/daemon/containerd/image_changes.go)
mounts both the parent image and the container root and calls
`archive.ChangesDirs(containerRoot, imageRoot)`. The call does not pass the
request context to the tree comparison. The endpoint returns the complete
change list; limiting the client's output therefore cannot bound the daemon's
tree-comparison allocation.

## Bounded diagnostic reproduction

Run on a disposable Linux VM with cgroup memory enforcement. Use a new DinD
daemon, without exposing the host Docker socket. Verify that `docker info`
inside it reports the containerd snapshotter. Cap the outer DinD container
at 1 GiB RAM, 1 GiB total memory/swap and 256 PIDs:

```sh
probe="dss-changes-probe-$$"
docker run -d --privileged --name "$probe" \
  --memory=1g --memory-swap=1g --pids-limit=256 \
  -e DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR= docker:29-dind
trap 'docker rm -f "$probe" >/dev/null' EXIT
ready=false
for attempt in $(seq 1 90); do
  if docker exec "$probe" docker info >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    ready=true
    break
  fi
  sleep 1
done
"$ready" || exit 1
docker exec "$probe" docker info
docker exec "$probe" sh -c '
  set -eu
  mkdir -p /tmp/context
  cat > /tmp/context/Dockerfile <<\EOF
FROM busybox:1.37
RUN mkdir /lower && i=0 && while [ "$i" -lt 10000 ]; do \
    echo lower > /lower/f"$i"; i=$((i+1)); done
EOF
  docker build -t changes-probe /tmp/context
  docker run -d --name target changes-probe sleep 600
  docker exec target sh -c "echo upper > /lower/one-new-file"
  time docker diff target > /tmp/diff-single.txt
  wc -l /tmp/diff-single.txt
'
```

The escaped heredoc delimiter preserves the Dockerfile variables literally.
This proposed diagnostic has not run here: our host rejects memory-capped DinD
containers with `cannot enter cgroupv2 ... invalid state` before startup.
Repeat with finite 1,000 and 10,000
lower files, and at most two concurrent requests. Record elapsed time and
the daemon's `/proc/<pid>/status` before/after; the diagnostic does not promise
to reproduce OOM. The memory cap contains any failure to this test daemon.
Wait for readiness before building; remove its container in `finally`/the trap.

## Workarounds and suggested code changes

Clients should serialize requests, cache one snapshot per measurement run,
skip large candidates or low-memory hosts, and prefer direct upperdir usage.
Removing image-layer files creates whiteouts and does not recover image bytes;
remove unused containers/images after work finishes instead.

For the overlay snapshotter, derive changes from upperdir metadata and whiteouts
without walking unchanged lower contents. For other snapshotters, add request
cancellation to tree comparison, bound concurrent expensive comparisons per
daemon, and expose a bounded/streaming changes API or snapshot usage suitable
for individual paths. Document that the current changes endpoint can consume
memory proportional to the compared trees.

title: Rootless: concurrent container starts race against host-namespace bind, fail with EADDRINUSE despite allocator OSAllocator retry
body:
### Description

When containers are started in rootless mode and request an ephemeral host port, container starts can fail with:

`error while calling RootlessKit PortManager.AddPort(): cannot expose port X: listen tcp 0.0.0.0:X: bind: address already in use`

Retrying the start usualy picks a different port and succeeds.

## Diagnosis

`daemon/libnetwork/portmappers/nat/mapper_linux.go::MapPorts` performs two distinct host-port binds:

1. `OSAllocator.RequestPortsInRange` (osallocator_linux.go) reserves a port in `portallocator`'s in-memory map and calls `bind(2)` (osallocator_linux.go) as a probe, retrying on EADDRINUSE (`maxAllocateAttempts`,osallocator_linux.go). Under rootless Docker, this bind happens in dockerd's network namespace, i.e. rootlesskit's *child* netns.

2. `configPortDriver` (mapper_linux.go) then calls `rlkclient.PortDriverClient.AddPort`, which makes rootlesskit perform a *second* bind in the host (parent) netns at `rootlesskit/pkg/port/builtin/parent/tcp/tcp.go`. On EADDRINUSE this error just propagates back to the API client, no retry (mapper_linux.go).

The two netns have separate kernel port tables. The retry in step 1 catches collisions in the child netns but provides no protection against host-netns collisions in step 2. The OSAllocator's bind probe verifies a port is free in the wrong network namespace.

## Proposed fix

Retry the allocate-and-bind cycle when `pdc.AddPort` reports EADDRINUSE. Sadly, the the IPC layer flattens errno into a string, so unless you're willing to do a coordinated API change this will require a sentinel inside the eror message string.

### Reproduce

```shell
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u

DOCKERD_PID="$(pgrep -x dockerd | head -1 || true)"
if [[ -z "$DOCKERD_PID" ]]; then
    echo "ERROR: dockerd not running" >&2; exit 1
fi
if [[ "$(readlink /proc/self/ns/net)" == "$(readlink /proc/"$DOCKERD_PID"/ns/net)" ]]; then
    echo "ERROR: this shell shares dockerd's netns — re-run from a plain user shell." >&2
    exit 1
fi

LO="${LO:-33000}"
HI="${HI:-33099}"
ITERATIONS="${ITERATIONS:-100}"
PARALLEL="${PARALLEL:-10}"
HOLD_S="${HOLD_S:-0.05}"
GAP_S="${GAP_S:-0.05}"
BACKOFF_S="${BACKOFF_S:-0.5}"
RETRY_BUDGET="${RETRY_BUDGET:-10}"

echo "attacking host ports $LO-$HI"

docker pull alpine:3 >/dev/null

python3 - "$LO" "$HI" "$HOLD_S" "$GAP_S" "$BACKOFF_S" <<'PY' &
import socket, sys, threading, time, random
lo, hi = int(sys.argv[1]), int(sys.argv[2])
HOLD_S, GAP_S, BACKOFF_S = float(sys.argv[3]), float(sys.argv[4]), float(sys.argv[5])
print(f"hammering host-netns ports {lo}-{hi} with one worker per port", flush=True)

def worker(port):
    time.sleep(random.uniform(0, HOLD_S + GAP_S))
    while True:
        try:
            s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
            s.bind(("0.0.0.0", port))
            s.listen(1)
        except OSError:
            time.sleep(BACKOFF_S)
            continue
        time.sleep(HOLD_S)
        s.close()
        time.sleep(GAP_S)

for port in range(lo, hi + 1):
    threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(port,), daemon=True).start()
while True:
    time.sleep(60)
PY
HAMMER_PID=$!
trap 'kill $HAMMER_PID 2>/dev/null' EXIT
sleep 0.5

echo "running $ITERATIONS docker iterations, up to $PARALLEL in parallel..."

export LO HI
results=$(seq 1 "$ITERATIONS" | xargs -P "$PARALLEL" -I{} bash -c '
    iter="$1"
    if out=$(docker run --rm -p "${LO}-${HI}:80" alpine:3 true 2>&1); then
        printf "iter %3d OK\n" "$iter"
    else
        printf "iter %3d FAIL: %s\n" "$iter" "$(echo "$out" | tr "\n" " " | sed "s/  */ /g")"
    fi
' _ {})

echo "$results"
fail=$(grep -c ' FAIL' <<<"$results")

echo
awk -v hold="$HOLD_S" -v gap="$GAP_S" -v retries="$RETRY_BUDGET" \
    -v fail="$fail" -v total="$ITERATIONS" \
    'BEGIN {
        p = hold / (hold + gap);
        printf "expected per-attempt failure rate:    %7.3f%%\n", p * 100;
        printf "expected after %dx retry (if fixed):   %7.3f%%\n", retries, (p^retries) * 100;
        printf "observed failure rate:                %7.3f%%  (%d/%d)\n", (fail/total) * 100, fail, total;
    }'

```

EDIT2: Added desync to hammer workers so the p^retries assumption holds.

### Expected behavior

Port allocation succeeds.

title: Container: network does not exist
body:
### Description

After upgrading to `29.7.0` or later, starting a container fails with the message:

```
Error response from daemon: failed to set up container networking: failed to create endpoint <container-name> on network br_docker: network 012e678a328601d4d8a4faaf423d499c5ac508de07ccfbee6c2ddc026c7e931f does not exist
```

However, if I do a `docker network inspect br_docker`, the network is there:
```
$ docker network ls                        
NETWORK ID     NAME            DRIVER    SCOPE
012e678a3286   br_docker       bridge    local
adfe7410062f   host            host      local
ac8f752236c8   mcvlan_docker   macvlan   local
a15c2b6385ed   none            null      local

$ docker network inspect br_docker      
[
    {
        "Name": "br_docker",
        "Id": "012e678a328601d4d8a4faaf423d499c5ac508de07ccfbee6c2ddc026c7e931f",
```

### Background

I run Docker with `iptables` and `ip6tables` disabled. I'm using firewalld, to filter traffic between zones. I am running Debian Trixie, with the latest updates.

This setup was very stable, but over time it degraded slowly:
- up to `29.6.x` everything was working fine
- upgrading to `29.7.x` showed the error, but re-recreating the custom bridge solved it permanently
- since `29.8.x`, re-recreating the bridge solves it temporary, but a restart of the host breaks it again
- `29.9.0`, no change in behavior compared to `29.8.x`

### Possible related issues

After searching, my issue looks a lot like:
https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/52642

But not completely. That issue exists since `29.4`, for me it regressed since `29.7` and `29.8`. 
As a test, I tried to set `DOCKER_TEST_NO_FIREWALLD`, this didn't fix it.

I have another `macvlan` network, which works fine. The issue seems to be on `bridge` networks only. 

I think this is a regression somewhere, or maybe a timing issue during start. I can reproduce it on another system.



### Reproduce

### Verify it works on 29.6.2:

1. On Debian Trixie, install `docker-ce=5:29.6.2-1~debian.13~trixie` and firewalld
2. Set `iptables:false` and `ip6tables:false` in `docker.json`
3. Create a custom bridge:
```
docker network create -d bridge \
    --subnet=172.18.0.0/16 \
    --gateway=172.18.0.1 \
    --opt com.docker.network.bridge.name=br_docker \
    br_docker
```

4. Assign this bridge to a firewalld zone:
```
firewall-cmd --new-zone=dockerbridge --permanent 
firewall-cmd --zone=dockerbridge --add-interface=br_docker --permanent
firewall-cmd --reload
```

5. Start a container with docker-compose:
```
services:
  test:
    image: caddy:alpine
    container_name: test
    networks:
      - br_docker
networks:
  br_docker:
    external: true
```

6. Restart the docker host, and observe the container starts perfectly fine, no errors.

### Upgrade to 29.7.2:

1. Upgrade the docker version: `docker-ce=5:29.7.2-1~debian.13~trixie`
2. Remove the container to be sure: `docker rm test`
3. Start the container, and observe the `network does not exist` error
4. Re-create the bridge
5. Start again, and observe the container starts normally
6. Reboot host, the container still starts normally

### Upgrade to `29.8.0` or later

1. Upgrade the docker version: `docker-ce=5:29.8.2-1~debian.13~trixie`
2. Remove the container to be sure: `docker rm test`
3. Start the container, and observe the `network does not exist` error
4. Re-create the bridge
5. Start again, and observe the container starts normally
6. Reboot host, notice the error is back after a reboot.

### Expected behavior

Docker should be able to start normally, without the `network cannot be found` error.

title: c8d: `docker image prune` deletes in-flight pulls' leases, corrupting concurrent pulls
body:
### Description

With the containerd image store enabled, `docker image prune` deletes the leases protecting **other, in-flight `docker pull` operations** and triggers a synchronous GC that removes their partially-ingested content. Concurrent pulls then fail with content-store errors that look like registry or filesystem corruption.

On a shared deploy host (~15 systemd timers, each running `docker pull` for its compose project once a minute, several ending in `docker image prune -f`), we saw hundreds of these failures per day, spread across every project. Removing the per-deploy prune (keeping a single nightly prune) reduced the failure count to zero immediately; nothing else changed. Concurrent pulls alone never raced — only pulls concurrent with a prune.

Observed failure signatures (all from the same mechanism, depending on where the victim pull is when the sweep hits):

```
failed commit on ref "manifest-sha256:…": commit failed: rename /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.content.v1.content/ingest/<id>/data /var/lib/containerd/io.containerd.content.v1.content/blobs/sha256/<digest>: no such file or directory
failed commit on ref "attestation-sha256:…"  (same rename error)
unable to lease content: lease does not exist: not found
NotFound: content digest sha256:<digest>: not found
failed to extract layer sha256:<digest>: … lchown … no such file or directory
```

A manual `docker pull` of the same tag succeeds instantly (it rarely lands inside a prune's sweep), which makes this easy to misdiagnose as registry flakiness.

### Mechanism (traced through source)

1. `PullImage` wraps the pull in a lease created by `withLease()` (`daemon/containerd/leases.go`), labelled `moby/prune.images=true` with an 8h expiry. That lease is the only thing protecting the pull's in-flight ingests and freshly-committed blobs.
2. `ImagePrune` (`daemon/containerd/image_prune.go`) lists leases by that same label (`pruneLeaseFilter`) and deletes **every one** — there is no check for whether a pull currently holds it — passing `leases.SynchronousDelete` on the last, which runs GC inline.
3. With the lease gone, the victim pull's ingest records are no longer GC roots; the sweep aborts the ingest (removing `/ingest/<id>` on disk) and deletes unreferenced blobs.
4. The victim's writer still holds the now-unlinked file descriptor, so writes keep succeeding until `Commit()` runs `os.Rename(ingest, target)` → `ENOENT` ("failed commit on ref …"). Depending on timing you instead get `lease does not exist` (attaching an existing blob to the just-deleted lease), `content digest … not found` (an already-committed blob swept before the image references it), or the `lchown` unpack failure (parent content collected mid-unpack).

The label-based delete was introduced in e6170a5c4 ("Fix lease management during image operations") and first shipped in v28.0.0; the code is unchanged on master. On 28.x it required opting into the containerd image store; since 29.0 the store is the default for fresh installs, so any host that runs pulls and prunes concurrently is exposed.

#51567 (closed, not reproduced) shows the same signatures on a CI autoscaler host — i.e. another machine running concurrent pulls and prunes.

### Reproduce

1. Docker Engine ≥ 29 (containerd image store enabled), any registry.
2. Loop A: `docker pull` a multi-layer image tag repeatedly (delete it locally between iterations, or pull several different tags).
3. Loop B: `docker image prune -f` every few seconds.
4. Loop A's pulls fail intermittently with the signatures above; without Loop B they never fail.

### Expected behavior

`docker image prune` should not affect concurrently running pulls. `ImagePrune` could skip leases that are currently referenced by an in-flight operation, or in-flight pulls could use a label distinct from the prunable one until they complete.

### docker version

Docker Engine – Community 29.5.2 (API 1.54), containerd.io 2.2.4, runc 1.3.5, Debian 13 (trixie), kernel 6.12.

### docker info (relevant excerpts)

```
Storage Driver: overlayfs
 driver-type: io.containerd.snapshotter.v1
```

No `/etc/docker/daemon.json` (all defaults); stock distro `/etc/containerd/config.toml` (`disabled_plugins = ["cri"]` only). containerd and dockerd had been running continuously for weeks (no restarts, no OOM, no disk pressure — 15% used, inodes 3%).

### Additional context

- containerd is behaving as instructed here — it GCs content whose lease moby deleted — so this does not reproduce via containerd alone; it needs moby's prune path.
- Attestation manifests (`attestation-sha256:…` refs from buildx provenance) widen the race window because the containerd store pulls and commits more blobs per image than the classic graph driver did, but the race is blob-agnostic: manifest, index, config, layer, and attestation refs all failed for us.

title: CopyToContainer racing AutoRemove fails with "RWLayer of container ... is unexpectedly nil" instead of a clean error
body:
### Description

When `docker cp` (CopyToContainer) runs concurrently with the auto-removal of the target
container (`docker create --rm` + `docker start` of a container that exits immediately),
the daemon fails the copy with:

```
Error response from daemon: RWLayer of container <id> is unexpectedly nil
```

instead of a graceful outcome. We would expect either a deterministic "No such container"
/ "container already removed" error, or (better, if feasible) for CopyToContainer on an
exited-but-not-yet-removed container to behave as it does for a still-running one — today
the window turns into this nil-RWLayer error.

This matters in practice: CI runners provision job containers exactly this way —
`docker create --rm` → `docker start` → copy the workspace in via CopyToContainer (that is
what Gitea Actions' runner and GitHub's self-hosted runner do). A job whose container exits
while the workspace copy is in flight fails spuriously with this daemon error, and we have
seen it take down CI jobs in the wild.

### Reproduce

Save as `race-probe.sh`, run anywhere against the affected daemon:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
iterations=40
rwlayer=0
blob_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
dd if=/dev/urandom of="$blob_dir/blob" bs=1M count=16 status=none
docker pull -q alpine:3.20 >/dev/null 2>&1
for i in $(seq 1 "$iterations"); do
  cid=$(docker create --rm alpine:3.20 true)
  ( docker start "$cid" >/dev/null 2>"$blob_dir/s.err" ) &
  starter=$!
  err=$(docker cp "$blob_dir/blob" "$cid:/probe-blob" 2>&1) || true
  wait "$starter" 2>/dev/null || true
  case "$err $(cat "$blob_dir/s.err" 2>/dev/null)" in
    *"RWLayer"*|*"unexpectedly nil"*) rwlayer=$((rwlayer+1)) ;;
  esac
done
rm -rf "$blob_dir"
echo "iterations=$iterations rwlayer_errors=$rwlayer"
```

Measured today, same script:

| host | daemon | platform / kernel | storage | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| VM (Oracle Cloud) | 29.8.0 | linux/arm64, 6.17.0-1019-oracle | overlayfs, containerd snapshotter | **17/40 failed** |
| homeserver | 29.8.2 | linux/amd64, 6.8.0-146-generic | overlayfs, containerd snapshotter | **16/40 failed** |

Error sample:

```
Error response from daemon: RWLayer of container 9ef313e3e3569ada63d6f32aea9351b415073f7740e774fccde15a28ab900c85 is unexpectedly nil
```

The rate scales with load; an idle machine still reproduces it eventually. It reproduces on
two architectures, two kernels and two recent daemon versions, so we do not believe this is
environment-specific.

### Additional info

- `moby/moby#49227` ("Goroutine panic and mutex leak in getInspectData") and its fix
  (#49228 / #49239, "Clear RWLayer reference under container lock") covered the **inspect**
  path; this report is the **CopyToContainer** path hitting the same nil-RWLayer window.
- Related open item: #53481 / #53512 (interrupted removal residue) — adjacent class.
- No other errors appear in `dockerd` logs; the container is removed normally.

```console
$ docker version
Client: Docker Engine - Community

Server: Docker Engine - Community

$ docker info (both hosts)

```

title: Swarm TaskDefaults.LogDriver is ignored by /swarm/update
body:
### Description

`TaskDefaults.LogDriver` is exposed as part of the swarm spec, but setting it through the Engine API does not persist the value.

`POST /swarm/update` accepts a spec containing `TaskDefaults.LogDriver` and returns success. Other fields included in the same update are persisted normally, but `TaskDefaults.LogDriver` is silently dropped. A subsequent `GET /swarm` returns an empty `TaskDefaults`.

I was trying to use this as a cluster-wide default log driver for swarm tasks where the service does not specify its own log driver.

Looking at the current Engine/SwarmKit conversion code, this appears to be a broken or incomplete Engine integration rather than an issue with the request format. `TaskDefaults` exists in the public Engine API types and in the underlying SwarmKit cluster spec, but the Engine conversion layer does not appear to map it in either direction.

### Reproduce

This can be reproduced with a single-node swarm.

1. Initialize a swarm if needed:

```bash
docker swarm init
```

2. Get the Engine API version and current swarm spec:

```bash
API_VERSION="$(docker version --format '{{.Server.APIVersion}}')"

curl -sS \
  --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock \
  "http://localhost/v${API_VERSION}/swarm" \
  > /tmp/swarm.json

VERSION="$(jq -r '.Version.Index' /tmp/swarm.json)"
```

3. Create an updated spec.

This changes `TaskHistoryRetentionLimit` as well as `TaskDefaults.LogDriver` so it is easy to verify that the update request itself is being applied:

```bash
jq '
  .Spec
  | .Orchestration.TaskHistoryRetentionLimit = 7
  | .TaskDefaults = {
      "LogDriver": {
        "Name": "json-file",
        "Options": {
          "max-size": "10m",
          "max-file": "3"
        }
      }
    }
' /tmp/swarm.json > /tmp/swarm-spec.json
```

Verify the request contains both values:

```bash
jq '{
  TaskHistoryRetentionLimit: .Orchestration.TaskHistoryRetentionLimit,
  TaskDefaults: .TaskDefaults
}' /tmp/swarm-spec.json
```

Output:

```json
{
  "TaskHistoryRetentionLimit": 7,
  "TaskDefaults": {
    "LogDriver": {
      "Name": "json-file",
      "Options": {
        "max-size": "10m",
        "max-file": "3"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

4. Submit the updated swarm spec:

```bash
curl -sS \
  --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock \
  -o /dev/null \
  -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \
  -X POST \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @/tmp/swarm-spec.json \
  "http://localhost/v${API_VERSION}/swarm/update?version=${VERSION}"
```

The request succeeds:

```text
HTTP 200
```

5. Read the swarm spec again:

```bash
curl -sS \
  --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock \
  "http://localhost/v${API_VERSION}/swarm" \
  | jq '{
      TaskHistoryRetentionLimit: .Spec.Orchestration.TaskHistoryRetentionLimit,
      TaskDefaults: .Spec.TaskDefaults
    }'
```

The regular swarm setting has been updated, but `TaskDefaults` has not:

```json
{
  "TaskHistoryRetentionLimit": 7,
  "TaskDefaults": {}
}
```

The same result can be seen by querying the field directly:

```bash
curl -sS \
  --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock \
```

This looks like a broken or incomplete Engine integration rather than an unsupported SwarmKit feature.

`TaskDefaults` still exists in the Engine API types, and `TaskDefaults.LogDriver` is documented there as the log driver used for tasks when a service does not specify one:

```text
api/types/swarm/swarm.go
```

However, the Engine's Swarm conversion code does not appear to handle `TaskDefaults` at all:

```text
daemon/cluster/convert/swarm.go
```

In particular, neither `SwarmFromGRPC()` nor `MergeSwarmSpecToGRPC()` appears to copy `TaskDefaults` between the Engine API types and the underlying SwarmKit cluster spec.

This seems to leave the implementation in a broken state:

- the Engine API exposes `TaskDefaults.LogDriver` as part of the swarm spec;
- SwarmKit has support for task defaults in its cluster spec;
- `/swarm/update` accepts a request containing `TaskDefaults.LogDriver` and returns success;
- but the Engine conversion layer drops the field before it reaches SwarmKit;
- and the reverse conversion also does not expose it through `GET /swarm`.

As a result, `TaskDefaults.LogDriver` is currently exposed through the Engine API but cannot actually be persisted or used through that API.

There is also some historical context in moby/moby#24476. When service-level log driver support was added, cluster-wide default log driver support for `docker swarm init` and `docker swarm update` was explicitly listed as remaining work. The discussion later says that cluster defaults would be handled separately.

SwarmKit's `TaskDefaults` structure was added around the same time in moby/swarmkit#1185.

Taken together, this looks like the Engine-side integration for cluster task defaults was never completed, while the corresponding public API types remained in place.

title: [29.9.0-rc.1 regression] docker pull fetches all layer blobs with stargz
body:
### Description

With stargz, `docker pull` on 29.9.0-rc.1 downloads all compressed layers even though the snapshotter prepares them remotely. Docker 29.8.2 avoids those full-layer downloads.

PR #53615 enables `WithUnpackFetchAllContent()` unconditionally. This correctly restores missing blobs needed for save/push, but also removes the download savings of lazy pulling.


### Reproduce

1. Run containerd v2.4.1 with stargz-snapshotter v0.18.2 registered as proxy snapshotter `stargz`, with `no_background_fetch = true`.
2. Set `"features": {"containerd-snapshotter": true}` and `"storage-driver": "stargz"` in the dockerd config (`daemon.json`).
3. Run `docker pull ghcr.io/stargz-containers/python:3.13-esgz`, then inspect layer blobs with `ctr --address <containerd-socket> --namespace moby content ls`.
4. Repeat the test with the official Docker 29.8.2 and 29.9.0-rc.1 builds. Keep the containerd and stargz versions the same, and start each run with clean Docker,
containerd, and stargz state.”



### Expected behavior

Allow snapshotter-managed pulls without fetching every compressed blob. An explicit opt-out could preserve the save/push fix by default, with the documented tradeoff that images may need missing blobs before they can be saved or pushed.

title: containerd image store: Lazily pulled images may lack full layer content with remote snapshotters
body:
- related: #49784 
- related: #53615
- related: #53864 

With a remote snapshotter (stargz, soci, nydus, overlaybd), `docker pull` doesn't download layer content that the snapshotter fetches lazily from the registry.

The images run, but `docker save` fails, and `docker push` fails unless the missing layers can be cross-repo mounted on the target registry.

This is basically #49784 was fixed by fetching all layer content on pull (#53615), and is intentionally reintroduced for remote snapshotters to keep the benefits of lazy pulling (https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/53877, #53864).


### Workaround

Set `"features": {"lazy-pull": false}` in `daemon.json`, reload the daemon configuration, and pull the image again.

title: pre-seeded tmpfs VOLUMES

### Description

A Dockerfile can name VOLUMES, and they will be pre-seeded by the images content. What if we want to make a VOLUME tmpfs, that we can preseed? E.g. i have a temp folder, that does include some preseeded data (and permissions)? every time the container starts, it starts in the same state.

Behind the scenes, this would be simply a tmpfs overlay on the image folder of course.

title: overlay: a failed container start can cut off other containers on the same node
body:
### Description

On a swarm overlay network, when a container fails to start on a node, a running container of the same network on that node can be cut off from the network. Its interface on the network goes down (`NO-CARRIER`). It can no longer reach other containers on the network, and they can no longer reach it.

libnetwork calls the overlay driver's `Leave` to roll back a failed join: once if `Join` failed, and twice if a later step failed. Each call decrements the join count of the network sandbox on the node. The count goes too low, and the driver destroys the sandbox (bridge and VXLAN device) while containers still use it.

### Reproduce

On a swarm manager (for example after `docker swarm init`):

```console
$ docker network create -d overlay --attachable ov
$ docker run -d --name c1 --network ov alpine sleep infinity
$ NS=/run/docker/netns/1-$(docker network inspect ov -f '{{slice .Id 0 10}}')
$ sudo ls $NS
/run/docker/netns/1-tkma4zmq1p
$ docker exec c1 ip link show eth0
1648: eth0@if1649: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP,M-DOWN> mtu 1450 qdisc noqueue state UP
```

Start two containers which fail after the overlay driver's `Join`. Here an invalid endpoint sysctl makes them fail:

```console
$ for i in 1 2; do docker run --rm --network name=ov,driver-opt=com.docker.network.endpoint.sysctls=net.ipv4.conf.IFNAME.no_such_setting=1 alpine true; done
docker: Error response from daemon: failed to set up container networking: failed to add interface veth187b52e to sandbox: /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/eth0/no_such_setting is not a sysctl file
docker: Error response from daemon: failed to set up container networking: failed to add interface vethc6dde2f to sandbox: /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/eth0/no_such_setting is not a sysctl file
$ sudo ls $NS
ls: cannot access '/run/docker/netns/1-tkma4zmq1p': No such file or directory
$ docker exec c1 ip link show eth0
1648: eth0@if1649: <NO-CARRIER,BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,M-DOWN> mtu 1450 qdisc noqueue state DOWN
```

Two failed starts are necessary here, because the load-balancer endpoint of the network (`ov-endpoint`) also holds a join on the node. A container on `ov` on another node can no longer ping `c1`.

### Expected behavior

`c1` keeps its connection to the network. The sandbox is destroyed only when the last container on the node leaves the network.

title: Startup noise from firewalld integration on every daemon start (COMMAND_FAILED flood + NAME_CONFLICT ERROR)
body:
# [Bug]: Startup noise from firewalld integration on every daemon start (COMMAND_FAILED flood + NAME_CONFLICT ERROR)

## Environment

- Host: Fedora Linux 44 (KDE Plasma), kernel 7.2.6-200.fc44.x86_64
- Docker: `docker-ce 29.8.1` (`Server Version: 29.8.1`), containerd 2.3.5, iptables 1.8.11 (nf_tables)
- firewalld: **2.4.4-1.fc44**
- Firewall backend: `iptables+firewalld`
- SELinux enforcing default; no `/etc/docker/daemon.json`

## What happened

On **every** boot (reproduced across 3 consecutive boots in one day), right after dockerd connects to firewalld over D-Bus, the journal is flooded with warnings from two overlapping causes:

### 1) firewalld: `WARNING: COMMAND_FAILED` — 64 warnings per boot

All of these are best-effort deletions of Docker chains that do not exist:

```
firewalld[...]: WARNING: COMMAND_FAILED: '/usr/sbin/iptables -w10 -t nat -D PREROUTING -m addrtype --dst-type LOCAL -j DOCKER' failed: iptables v1.8.11 (nf_tables): Chain 'DOCKER' does not exist
firewalld[...]: WARNING: COMMAND_FAILED: '/usr/sbin/iptables -w10 -t nat -F DOCKER' failed: iptables: No chain/target/match by that name.
firewalld[...]: WARNING: COMMAND_FAILED: '/usr/sbin/iptables -w10 -t filter -F DOCKER-FORWARD' failed: iptables: No chain/target/match by that name.
... (DOCKER-BRIDGE, DOCKER-CT, DOCKER-INTERNAL, DOCKER-ISOLATION-STAGE-1/2, DOCKER-ISOLATION, DOCKER-INGRESS; same for ip6tables)
```

Count is deterministic: 32 IPv4 + 32 IPv6 = 64, i.e. one `-D`/`-F`/`-X` per chain per family.

### 2) firewalld: `ERROR: NAME_CONFLICT: new_policy_object(): 'docker-forwarding'`

```
firewalld[...]: ERROR: NAME_CONFLICT: new_policy_object(): 'docker-forwarding'
```

### 3) dockerd (INFO level, minor)

```
dockerd: msg="Deleting nftables IPv4 rules" error="..." output="... delete table ip docker-bridges"
dockerd: msg="Deleting nftables IPv6 rules" error="..." output="... delete table ip6 docker-bridges"
```

## Root cause analysis (from source on master)

1. **COMMAND_FAILED flood** — `daemon/libnetwork/drivers/bridge/internal/iptabler/iptabler.go`, `NewIptabler()` calls `removeIPChains(ctx, ipv)` **unconditionally** at every daemon start (both IPv4 and IPv6), before `setupIPChains()`. `removeIPChains` issues `-D`/`-F`/`-X` for all legacy Docker chains via firewalld's `direct.passthrough`. On a clean boot those chains don't exist, so every command fails and firewalld logs each failure at WARNING (`passthrough ... Possible errors: COMMAND_FAILED`). Docker intentionally ignores these errors and then recreates the chains. Result: pure log noise, no functional impact.

2. **NAME_CONFLICT ERROR** — `daemon/libnetwork/iptables/firewalld.go`, `setupDockerForwardingPolicy()` calls `org.fedoraproject.FirewallD1.config.addPolicy` **without first checking whether the policy exists** (the zone path `setupDockerZone()` *does* pre-check via `getZones`, so it only emits INFO). Because the permanent `docker-forwarding` policy already exists (created on the first run), firewalld raises `NAME_CONFLICT` and logs it at ERROR/journal level. Docker handles it correctly (catches `NAMECONFLICT`-prefixed `FirewallD1.Exception`, logs at DEBUG "policy already exists"), but the firewalld-side ERROR still lands in the journal every boot.

3. **nft table delete (INFO)** — cleanup of the leftover `docker-bridges`/`docker-bridges-ip6` nft tables on restore; table absent after firewalld has already handled it. Benign; also reported by other 29.x users (e.g. Home Assistant OS dockerd 29.4.1).

## Expectation

Startup should not emit error/warning floods for an idempotent, expected condition. Suggested fixes (any combination):

- In `NewIptabler`, only call `removeIPChains` when evidence of a previous daemon exists (e.g. gate on a `-C`/`Exists` check like `NewCleaner` does), or otherwise treat ENOENT/`No chain/target/match by that name` as success.
- In `setupDockerForwardingPolicy`, pre-check `## config.listPolicies()` (or `listPolicies` on the config D-Bus object) before `addPolicy`, mirroring the zone path, so no NAME_CONFLICT is raised at all.

## Current behavior (what actually works)

Despite all warnings, runtime state is correct on every boot:

- `docker` zone active (target ACCEPT) on `docker0` and bridge networks, runtime + permanent.
- `docker-forwarding` policy active (ingress ANY, egress docker, target ACCEPT).
- Containers publish ports normally (IPv4/IPv6), container egress/DNS works, no failed systemd units.

title: awslogs: identify concurrent writer to outgoing CloudWatch request headers
body:
- related to: https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/53273

Windows unit CI intermittently reports a concurrent access to the client-side `http.Request.Header` while sending a CloudWatch Logs request:

```text
fatal error: concurrent map read and map write

net/http.Header.sortedKeyValues
net/http.Header.writeSubset
net/http.(*Request).write
net/http.(*persistConn).writeLoop
```

The failure was discovered through `TestNewAWSLogsClientUserAgentHandler` and is tracked as test flakiness in #53273. PR #53322 isolates that test from the real HTTP transport, but does not identify or fix the concurrent writer.

Production awslogs requests use the same AWS SDK and Go HTTP transport path, so the underlying request ownership race should be tracked separately.

### Current findings

- The stack identifies `net/http` reading the header map, but does not include the writer stack.
- The `httptest.Server` cannot mutate this map because it receives a separately parsed server-side request.
- Moby and AWS middleware normally update headers before Smithy calls `http.Request.Clone` and hands the cloned request to `net/http`.
- The failure has not reproduced reliably under repeated race-detector runs.
- No request-path source changes were found in the AWS dependency update associated with one failing CI run.

It is therefore not yet known whether the writer is in Moby, AWS/Smithy, an HTTP wrapper, or Go’s HTTP client.

title: Windows layer export fails with `unknown stream ID 9` for sparse `DO*.tmp` file on Windows 26H1
body:
### Description

A Windows container build consistently fails while Docker commits a layer containing a sparse temporary file created during Visual Studio 2022 Build Tools installation.

The installation command completes successfully. Docker then fails during layer export with:

```text
re-exec error: Files/Windows/Temp/DOBDAB.tmp: unknown stream ID 9
```

Windows defines backup stream ID `9` as `BACKUP_SPARSE_BLOCK`.

### Reproduction

```dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/windows/server:ltsc2022

RUN powershell Set-ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope Process -Force; iex ((New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadString('https://chocolatey.org/install.ps1'))
RUN choco install -y --no-progress visualstudio2022buildtools
RUN choco install -y --no-progress visualstudio2022-workload-vctools && powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "$files = @(Get-ChildItem 'C:\Windows\Temp' -Filter 'DO*.tmp' -File -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue); Write-Host ('DIAG DO_COUNT=' + $files.Count); foreach ($file in $files) { Write-Host ('DIAG PATH=' + $file.FullName); Write-Host ('DIAG LENGTH=' + $file.Length); Write-Host ('DIAG ATTRIBUTES=' + $file.Attributes); fsutil.exe sparse queryflag $file.FullName }"
```

Build command:

```powershell
docker build --memory 8g --no-cache --pull -t windows-sparse-repro .
```

### Actual behavior

The workload installation succeeds:

```text
visualstudio2022-workload-vctools has been installed.
The install of visualstudio2022-workload-vctools was successful.
Chocolatey installed 8/8 packages.
```

The diagnostic confirms that one sparse temporary file was created:

```text
DIAG DO_COUNT=1
DIAG PATH=C:\Windows\Temp\DOBDAB.tmp
DIAG LENGTH=0
DIAG ATTRIBUTES=Archive, SparseFile
This file is set as sparse
```

Docker then fails while exporting that same file:

```text
re-exec error: Files/Windows/Temp/DOBDAB.tmp: unknown stream ID 9: output: 9148239275
```

The system had approximately 127 GB free, so this does not appear to be a disk-space failure.

### Expected behavior

Docker should successfully commit a layer containing this valid NTFS sparse file, or otherwise handle the `BACKUP_SPARSE_BLOCK` representation returned by Windows.

### Environment

```text
Docker Desktop: 4.87.0 (236836)
Docker Engine: 29.7.2
Engine commit: 6a43e3d
API version: 1.55
Go version: go1.26.5
Storage driver: windowsfilter
Docker root: C:\ProgramData\Docker
Host OS: Microsoft Windows Version 26H1
Host build: 28000.2704
Container base: mcr.microsoft.com/windows/server:ltsc2022
```

The original build failure was reproduced on two separate machines using the same Docker version. The focused diagnostic above was run on one of them.

### Suspected implementation area

Docker Engine commit `6a43e3d` vendors:

```text
github.com/Microsoft/go-winio
v0.6.3-0.20251027160822-ad3df93bed29
```

The vendored `backuptar` implementation only accepts `BackupSparseBlock` in its expected sparse-data sequence. Other occurrences reach:

```go
default:
    return fmt.Errorf("%s: unknown stream ID %d", name, bhdr.Id)
```

References:

- [Docker's vendored `go-winio/backuptar`](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/6a43e3d5afddf4111da0f864bbc7cae5d7e95001/vendor/github.com/Microsoft/go-winio/backuptar/tar.go)
- [`go-winio` sparse handling PR #221](https://github.com/microsoft/go-winio/pull/221)
- [Microsoft `WIN32_STREAM_ID` documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/ns-winbase-win32_stream_id)

PR #221 describes a previous Windows change that altered sparse backup-stream representations and broke `backuptar`. This may be another unhandled representation exposed by Windows 26H1.

An independent report describes the same `unknown stream ID 9` failure for a sparse Windows Update cache file:

- [Notes from week 34: Inside the Windows workers](https://www.tunbury.org/2026/08/24/week-34-2025/#inside-the-windows-workers)

title: Windows: containerd image store can't use the CimFS snapshotter — dockerd doesn't configure the differ order and offers no passthrough
body:
### Summary
On Windows, Docker's containerd image store can *select* the `cimfs` snapshotter but **cannot pull/unpack** into it, because dockerd's managed containerd is configured with the default diff-service differ order and there's no way to change it. containerd itself fully supports CimFS today — the gap is entirely in how dockerd generates (and locks down) the managed containerd config.

### Environment
- Windows 11 25H2 (build 10.0.26200), Docker Engine 29, dockerd-managed containerd **v2.3.1**.
- Image store enabled: `daemon.json` → `"default-runtime": "io.containerd.runhcs.v1"`, `"features": { "containerd-snapshotter": true }`.

### What works: containerd + CimFS end-to-end (via `ctr`)
containerd ships a complete `cimfs` snapshotter (`plugins/snapshots/windows/cimfs.go`) **and** a complete `cimfs` differ (`plugins/diff/windows/cimfs.go`, `ImportCimLayerFromTar`). Both load on 26200 (`IsCimFSSupported()` = true). With a standalone containerd whose config wires cimfs into the two relevant places:

```toml
[plugins."io.containerd.service.v1.diff-service"]
  default = ["cimfs", "windows", "windows-lcow"]

[[plugins."io.containerd.transfer.v1.local".unpack_config]]
  platform = "windows/amd64"
  snapshotter = "windows"
  differ = "windows"
[[plugins."io.containerd.transfer.v1.local".unpack_config]]
  platform = "windows/amd64"
  snapshotter = "cimfs"
  differ = "cimfs"
```

…a full pull → unpack → run works:

```
ctr --address <pipe> images pull --snapshotter cimfs mcr.microsoft.com/windows/nanoserver:ltsc2025   # unpacks via the cimfs differ
ctr --address <pipe> run --rm --snapshotter cimfs mcr.microsoft.com/windows/nanoserver:ltsc2025 t cmd /c "echo ok"   # -> ok
```

The runhcs shim mounts the CimFS rootfs (`rootfs type=CimFS`, `mountProcessIsolatedCimLayersCommon`) and the container runs. So the snapshotter, differ, and runtime are all functional on GA Windows.

### What fails: the same thing under dockerd
`DOCKER_DRIVER=cimfs` (the Windows way to pick a non-default snapshotter — `daemon/image_store_choice.go`) makes `docker info` report `Driver=cimfs` and dockerd starts, but any pull fails at unpack:

```
failed to extract layer ... to cimfs ...: Unimplemented: mount layer type must be lcow-layer: not implemented
```

### Root cause
dockerd's own pull-unpack goes through the containerd **diff service**, whose Windows default order is hardcoded to `["windows", "windows-lcow"]` (`plugins/services/diff/service_windows.go`). The `cimfs` differ is registered but never in that order, so a `CimFSMountType` mount is rejected by `windows` (wants `windows-layer`) then `windows-lcow` (wants `lcow-layer`) — that last rejection is the error above.

The order is only fixable via containerd config, but:
- dockerd generates the managed `containerd.toml` purely from an internal struct and applies only a few `DaemonOpt`s (log level/format, CRI-disable, local-binary detection — `daemon/internal/libcontainerd/supervisor/remote_daemon*.go`); **none touch the diff-service or transfer plugins**.
- There is **no daemon.json field** to inject containerd plugin config.
- The file is rewritten (`O_TRUNC`) on every daemon start, so hand-edits don't survive.

So today there is no supported way to make dockerd use CimFS, even though every underlying piece works.

### Why it matters
CimFS mounts read-only `.cim` layer files instead of expanding each layer on disk — a meaningful storage/space win for WCOW images (relevant to the long-standing "Windows images use far more disk than their actual size" complaint) and potentially faster layer setup.

### Proposed fix (options)
1. **Auto-wire** — when the selected image-store snapshotter is a CIM snapshotter, add the matching differ (`cimfs`, and `blockcim` when available) to the managed containerd's diff-service order (and transfer `unpack_config`).
2. **Passthrough** — let operators supply extra containerd plugin config that dockerd merges into the managed `containerd.toml` (would also unblock other snapshotters).

### Forward note: blockcim is already implemented in containerd
The same containerd file registers a `blockcim` snapshotter/differ, and it's complete — it just skip-loads on current GA Windows because hcsshim gates it to build ≥ 27766 (`IsBlockCimSupported()`, an explicit placeholder pending an official build; verified/merged CIM ≥ 27800). So once Windows ships block-CIM support, **no new containerd work is needed** — only the *same* dockerd wiring this issue asks for. Designing the fix to cover both `cimfs` and `blockcim` now avoids a second round later.

### Upstream context
Filed a companion issue on containerd proposing it default-wire these snapshotters when the OS supports them (so this stops being per-downstream boilerplate): containerd/containerd#13782.

title: Enable SELinux support for overlay2 in rootless mode
body:
### Description

When running rootless docker on fedora, it uses fuse-overlayfs by default, and trying to manually switch to overlay2 says it's not supported with selinux.
This issue https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/42333 mentions that using overlay2 in rootless doesn't work when selinux is enabled. Unsure what's the os that was used for the test, but supposedly it should cause permission denied errors related to selinux when trying to run any container including hello world, and that's why it was gated in dockerd itself.
However here on my os (fedora 41, kernel 6.15) this permission denied error doesn't happen anymore when running hello-world. Can that be reconsidered or changed so that it affects only systems where it actually fails?
On a side note, there is code in the rootless script that changes selinux context on /run so that iptables is happy, and it also seems not needed anymore or not with iptables-nft.

### Reproduce

These repro steps are valid on fedora-41, but might not work on rhel/centos or older fedora so needs verification.
1. Remove docker data or manually switch to overlay2 driver in daemon.json, but don't start docker yet.
2. Temporarily comment selinux detection logic in docker-rootless.sh script:
   ```
   #	if command -v selinuxenabled > /dev/null 2>&1 && selinuxenabled; then
   #		_DOCKERD_ROOTLESS_SELINUX=1
   #		export _DOCKERD_ROOTLESS_SELINUX
   #	fi
   ```
3. Now, run dockerd with `systemctl --user start docker`
4. Use `docker info` and verify docker successfully started with overlay2.
5. Run `docker run --rm hello-world` as in the above mentioned issue.
6. Observe it working even though according to above issue, it shouldn't.
7. Try doing: `dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh nsenter`.
8. Now, do `iptables -L`.
9. See it also works, although unsure if it was enough to trigger the other, iptables related selinux issue.

### Expected behavior

This shouldn't require disabling the selinux detection logic.

title: Docker Swarm stack update loses published ports when VIP IP alias already exists
body:
### Description

When updating a Docker Swarm stack service that publishes ports, the update can fail silently if the VIP IP alias already exists on the LB endpoint interface. The daemon logs show a file exists error from AddAliasIP, and the service ends up without any published ports accessible.

This occurs even though the service task itself is running, leading to a loss of connectivity for clients.

### Reproduce

1. Create a minimal stack YAML (/tmp/docker-compose.yml):
```yaml
services:
  whoami:
    image: containous/whoami:latest
    deploy:
      update_config:
        order: start-first
    ports:
      - "8181:80"
      - "8881:80"

networks:
  default:
    driver: overlay
```
2. Deploy the stack:
```
docker stack deploy -c /tmp/docker-compose.yml test
sudo netstat -tpnl | grep dockerd
```
Observe both ports (8181, 8881) are listening.
3. Change one published port in the YAML, e.g.:
```
sed -i 's/8181/8182/' /tmp/docker-compose.yml
docker stack deploy -c /tmp/docker-compose.yml test
sudo netstat -tpnl | grep dockerd
```
4. Check daemon logs and notice:
```
level=error msg="Failed add IP alias 10.0.0.X to network <ingress-net> LB endpoint interface eth0: file exists"
```
Ports previously mapped (8181, 8881) are now gone.


### Expected behavior

- Updating a stack with changed published ports should update port bindings correctly.
- Docker should handle the case where the VIP IP alias already exists without removing previously published ports.
- Logs should report a non-fatal debug message when the alias already exists, without interrupting the update rollout.

title: Swarm service unable to connect to host IP since 29.8.0
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/moby/moby/discussions/53709
Originally posted by **JoshStark** September 17, 2026 Thought I'd open a discussion as this change seems deliberate based on my (limited) understanding of this PR which was included in the `29.8.0` release. https://github.com/moby/moby/pull/53118 Since updating our Swarm cluster to `29.8.0` we have observed that services running on any particular node are no longer able to connect to other services running on that same node when using the node's host IP address; either directly or via a FQDN. Our Swarm cluster is structured with 4 nodes: 1x manager, 3x workers, with services deployable to any one of the 4 nodes. Our general approach has been to use a reverse proxy (Traefik in this case) to resolve requests from services both on and off the Swarm to allow connectivity to other services running on the swarm. Traefik runs exclusively on the manager node, so if a service which is also on the manager makes a request to another service which is running on the manager will resolve to the manager's host IP address, which no longer routes successfully on `29.8.0`, but it did work on `29.7.2`. I guess this question comes down to one of best practices and whether this change is a regression or if best practices dictate that services running on a Swarm should not be able to do this. If the destination service was running on another one of the worker nodes then the request will have been fulfilled. Was this change intended? Non-swarm Docker hosts do not seem affected by this change, as I've tried the same on a standard Docker host which still allows routing via the host IP from one service to another. Thanks.
-------- When the userland proxy is disabled, a Swarm task is unable to reach another task on the same node via a published port on any of the host's IP addresses as of Docker 29.8.0.

title: Overlay MTU is 20 bytes too large on an IPv6 Swarm data path
body:
### Description

The overlay driver sets a container's overlay interface MTU to the network's base MTU (1500 unless `com.docker.network.driver.mtu` is set) minus a fixed 50-byte VXLAN allowance. The allowance assumes an IPv4 outer header. On an IPv6 Swarm data path the overhead is 70 bytes:

| Header | Allowance | IPv6 data path |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Inner Ethernet | 14 | 14 |
| Outer IP | 20 | 40 |
| UDP | 8 | 8 |
| VXLAN | 8 | 8 |
| Total | 50 | 70 |

The container's MTU is therefore 20 bytes larger than the path can carry.

On a 1500-byte underlay the container's interface MTU is 1450, but with the don't-fragment bit set only packets up to 1430 bytes cross between nodes. Anything sized to the interface MTU, TCP's MSS included, is 20 bytes too large for the path.

In my test the 1450-byte DF send failed with `EMSGSIZE` because the sending container's kernel had already learned the lower path MTU. Full-size packets depend on path MTU discovery to get through.

### Reproduce

1. Two Linux hosts with IPv6 connectivity to each other, on a network with a 1500-byte MTU.
2. On host 1: `docker swarm init --advertise-addr <host1-ipv6>`
3. On host 2: `docker swarm join --advertise-addr <host2-ipv6> --token <token> [<host1-ipv6>]:2377`
4. On host 1:
   ```
   docker network create -d overlay --attachable ov
   docker run -d --name target --network ov alpine sleep infinity
   ```
5. On host 2:
   ```
   docker run --rm --network ov alpine sh -c '
     cat /sys/class/net/eth0/mtu
     apk add -q iputils
     ping -c1 -W2 -M do -s 1402 target  # 1430-byte IP packet
     ping -c1 -W2 -M do -s 1422 target  # 1450-byte IP packet
   '
   ```

The interface MTU is 1450. The first ping gets a reply. The second fails.

An IPv4 control plane with an IPv6 `--data-path-addr` gives the same result.

### Expected behavior

The overlay interface MTU is the largest packet that crosses the data path: 1430 on a 1500-byte IPv6 underlay.

### docker version

The bug is in every release since v25.0.0, which added IPv6 data-path support (#46790), and on master.

### docker info

The bug does not depend on the environment beyond an IPv6 data-path address.

### Additional Info

- The allowance is `vxlanEncap = 50` in `daemon/libnetwork/drivers/overlay/overlay.go`. It is subtracted in `(*network).maxMTU`, which sets both the VXLAN link's MTU and the container's interface MTU. The kernel's allowance for VXLAN over IPv6 is 70 bytes (`VXLAN6_HEADROOM`).
- Encrypted overlays subtract the same allowance before the ESP overhead. On an IPv6 data path they should get an MTU of 1424 where the path fits 1404 (1500 − 70 − 26). I have not measured this.
- Workaround: create the network with `com.docker.network.driver.mtu` set 20 bytes below the underlay MTU, e.g. `--opt com.docker.network.driver.mtu=1480` on a 1500-byte underlay. The allowance is subtracted from that value, giving 1430, or 1404 on an encrypted network.
- `setupSubnetSandbox` calls `isIPv6Transport()` to configure the VXLAN link for IPv6 peers. `maxMTU` could choose its allowance the same way.

title: docker pull/push rejects IPv6 link-local literal with zone ID ([fe80::...%eth0]:5000/image): "invalid reference format"
body: ### Description IPv6 address literals in image references are accepted since the fix from distribution/distribution#3489 (see #39033), e.g. [::1]:5000/image. However, a link-local IPv6 address with a zone ID is still rejected by the reference parser, so it is impossible to push/pull to a registry reachable only via IPv6 link-local. Use case: several devices on a network with only static link-local IPv6. One device runs an OCI registry (registry:3, host networking, listening on *:5000), the others need to pull/push. Global/ULA addresses are not available. The error comes from the reference parser, before any network connection is attempted. The registry itself is reachable over link-local (curl works, see below). ### Reproduce 1. Run a registry on the host: docker run -d --network host registry:3 2. Run: $ docker pull '[fe80::215:5dff:fea0:7253%eth0]:5000/test:latest' invalid reference format ### Expected behavior The reference is accepted and the client connects to https://[fe80::...%25eth0]:5000/v2/ (zone ID percent-encoded per RFC 6874), or a documented alternative syntax exists for link-local registries. ### docker version ```bash 29.8.1 / 29.8.1 ``` ### docker info ```bash docker info Client: Docker Engine - Community Version: 29.8.1 Context: default Debug Mode: false Plugins: buildx: Docker Buildx (Docker Inc.) Version: v0.37.1 Path: /usr/libexec/docker/cli-plugins/docker-buildx compose: Docker Compose (Docker Inc.) Version: v5.5.1 Path: /usr/libexec/docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose Server: Containers: 4 Running: 2 Paused: 0 Stopped: 2 Images: 8 Server Version: 29.8.1 Storage Driver: overlay2 Backing Filesystem: extfs Supports d_type: true Using metacopy: false Native Overlay Diff: true userxattr: false Logging Driver: json-file Cgroup Driver: systemd Cgroup Version: 2 Plugins: Volume: local ``` ### Additional Info Suggested direction: allow an optional zone ID in the IPv6 literal of the reference domain regexp (e.g. [fe80::1%25eth0]) and make sure the registry client percent-encodes it when building the URL (Go's net/url and net.Dialer handle zone IDs). If out of scope, a docs note that link-local zone IDs are unsupported would help.

title: exec exit handler blocks forever in unbuffered.Clean(), wedging all further events for that container
body: ### Description When a client attaches to an exec and then stops reading, the exec's exit event handler in the daemon blocks forever, and because libcontainerd serialises containerd events per container ID, every subsequent event for that container is stuck behind it. The container keeps working for anything that does not go through the event stream (`ps`, `top`, `logs`, `inspect`, `stats`), but no further exec ever completes and the container's own exit event never lands. Other containers are unaffected. The blocking pair, in `daemon/monitor.go` `EventExit` for an exec ([monitor.go:226](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/c3065211177705ada59a9ccf8b5c182f286f8c97/daemon/monitor.go#L226-L232)): ```go ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Second) execConfig.StreamConfig.Wait(ctx) cancel() if err := execConfig.CloseStreams(); err != nil { ``` That 2 second bound came in with b5f28865 ("Handle blocked I/O of exec'd processes", 2019) precisely so a stuck exec could not hold up the handler. The next line removes the bound again. `CloseStreams` calls `unbuffered.Clean`, which takes the broadcaster mutex, and that mutex is held across a blocking write ([unbuffered.go:23-49](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/c3065211177705ada59a9ccf8b5c182f286f8c97/daemon/internal/stream/unbuffered.go#L23-L49)): ```go func (w *unbuffered) Write(p []byte) (int, error) { w.mu.Lock() var evict []int for i, sw := range w.writers { if n, err := sw.Write(p); err != nil || n != len(p) { // blocks here, mutex held ... func (w *unbuffered) Clean() error { w.mu.Lock() // never returns ``` The attached client's writer is a `bytespipe`, which blocks its writer once `bufLen >= blockThreshold` (1e6). So when the client stops draining the attach connection, the stdout copier parks inside `unbuffered.Write` with the mutex held, and the exit handler parks in `unbuffered.Clean` waiting for it. `StreamConfig.Wait`'s own timeout path cannot break this. On `ctx.Done()` it calls `dio.Cancel()`, `dio.Wait()`, `dio.Close()` ([streams.go:170-185](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/c3065211177705ada59a9ccf8b5c182f286f8c97/daemon/internal/stream/streams.go#L170-L185)), all of which act on the containerd fifo side. The copier is not blocked reading the fifo, it is blocked writing to the client-side pipe, so closing the fifo changes nothing. `Wait` returns after 2 seconds as designed and the handler then blocks in `CloseStreams` instead. Goroutine dump from a wedged daemon (29.8.0), with the daemon build path stripped and one argument list elided. The receiver address `0xf6eacf34560` is the same `unbuffered` in both stacks: ``` goroutine 319918 [sync.Cond.Wait, 2 minutes]: sync.runtime_notifyListWait(0xf6eac8c9ed0, 0x9) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/sema.go:617 +0x1b3 sync.(*Cond).Wait(0x5dbd3e0e75b8?) /usr/local/go/src/sync/cond.go:71 +0x73 github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon/internal/stream/bytespipe.(*BytesPipe).Write(0xf6eaaa0d6d0, {0xf6eabd74000?, 0x5dbd38fdf110?, 0xf6eacf87680?}) daemon/internal/stream/bytespipe/bytespipe.go:92 +0x3bc github.com/moby/moby/v2/daemon/internal/stream.(*unbuffered).Write(0xf6eacf34560, {0xf6eabd74000, 0x8000, 0x8000}) daemon/internal/stream/unbuffered.go:27 +0x10e io.copyBuffer({0x5dbd3e0ec1c0, 0xf6eacf34560}, {0x79ee5c2d2758, 0xf6eacf87440}, {0xf6eabd74000, 0x8000, 0x8000}) /usr/local/go/src/io/io.go:431 +0x1d4 io.CopyBuffer(...) /usr/local/go/src/io/io.go:402 +0x36
